seriously? I’m not talking specifically about city builders, because they know almost nothing about transportation either; but a lot of people who think that it’s all right if we go back to medieval levels of living standards for most people … or something.

The main problem with “building city nations”, as I see it, isn’t just that any such undertaking would require enormous effort from government and private resources (though that is certainly true). Nor is simply that people will resent those efforts – though that may also be true. Nope: what’s really driving me up the wall is the belief that (some sort) of national infrastructure project was necessary, because otherwise everything is just too bad.

The thing is, there are lots of things which are bad — politics, an environment increasingly dominated by free-riders, sedentary citizens who don’t feel connected to each other – and yet the underlying problem is not the result of ‘nationalism’ per se, but poor design decisions on both the local and state level … and yes, national infrastructure projects could do some damage at worst even when they’re built properly, as in New South Wales recently. In many cases states could do better by simply improving existing bus systems and rail networks.

Now, of course, there are situations where good public policy and competent government might fail to adequately address certain needs (like subsidized water delivery during prolonged drought), but this is not an example of failure in standard political economics theory.

And then of course there are instances like developed areas where the total number of people multiplied against horrendously unfavourable land use per capita means that everyone has to pay high taxes so that someone else in another region in the same country can ignore the problems of self-imposed poverty perpetuated by subsidies, tipping them towards becoming another Hottentot desert where no one cares more than themselves. This isn’t just stupid, it’s actually counterproductive given the benefits of globalization.

So here’s how I think transportation systems work. Here:

  • People drive cars.
  • Then they look around, and realize that if car travel wasn’t cheap, they’d never own cars.
  • Therefore, subsidizing and encouraging personal mode of mobility has more long term economic benefit than eliminating individual freedom to move about without an expensive car through public transit
  • However, having said all that, we have reason to invest real money in proper road construction, highway maintenance, and smart traffic management. Otherwise we risk disaster, as happened during Hurricane Katrina.

However, Sorenstam, who just completed her fifth straight victory in major championships, also knows how to keep herself busy. She recently earned $2 million and became worth about $38 million after selling a piece of stock valued at nearly $4 million and adding more than $400,000 to her savings account from working at FedEx.
She had been counting on getting pull tabs or additional job opportunities from a sponsorship tie-in but decided against it as a way of keeping costs low and expenses down.
"There are enough jobs out there, so I won't need to go shopping every week for another swing bag, and I won't have to spend money on those kinds of things," she said.
Sorenstam played at the Valero Texas Open, the Honda Classic and the Valspar Championship, all without official tournament sponsorships for companies. Her second-place finish and the $275,000 check are among five large payouts out of seven wins in 2003 and help position her to challenge Vijay Singh for the Women's World Golf Ranking title.
Sorentam told the media her financial situation wasn't as tough as it appeared because most sponsors pay their employees through payroll deductions. However, the amount paid can add up over a long period of time to total tens of thousands of dollars.
Sorenstam, whose career earnings grew to about $2.5 million from less than $300,000 four years ago, has been holding back until late March or early April before making any selections.
Her tagline since the beginning of the year has been: ""I'm not ready yet."'

Sorenstam hoped to get on court at least once or twice before the multihour days of July and August, which normally bring good crowds to sports venues around the country.

2017 presidential election was hailed by proponents as one that had set national standards for free, fair and credible elections across Africa – even though its outcome may have given credence to critics’ arguments that “freedom” meant nothing new or different from what existed before (i.e., an oligarchy with a long history of rule through violence). Whether or not this is the case remains open to debate. Regardless of whether we celebrate or condemn, we must acknowledge that changes do take place in politics when democracy moves beyond rhetoric into the realm of reality.
Some who champion democracy today claim they know how to do so: there are rules, practices and procedures which ensure fairness (or at least make attempts at doing so) and thereby prevent abuses. They argue that democracy means having thresholds where power cannot be arbitrarily seized or distributed. In short, political elites need to give up too much control over their destiny, and the public can get involved if necessary to stop them.
But these assertions rest on shaky foundations. For one thing, many democratic leaders share scant knowledge about democratic institutions; they think, and act accordingly, as “unworthy” candidates should. Second, current democracies around the world, including Kenya, show no signs of giving away too much power; rather, the reverse appears true. Third, although transparency and accountability are essential features of modern global citizenship, few people would agree that any number of politicians being held accountable for their actions makes an otherwise undemocratic system more democratic. Fourth, increasing influence of consensus-based, multi-issue parties that speak for all citizens or majorities has been accompanied by increased polarization among traditional party factions within those parties. Hence, as one activist put it, indeed, “too many people will vote for any candidate.” In other words, the extension of democracy does not always bring us closer together, but often pushes citizens further apart.
It is clear from my experience around the region (including with colleagues at AU/ICG), that internal actors – governments, non-governmental organizations, business, labour unions and youth groups– play a central role in determining the success or failure of elections. To understand why that is the case requires more than simply recounting past events and the results they produced. I propose therefore focusing our attention on four aspects:
First, we have to question the assumption that mechanisms to counter corruption and abuse of power via checks-and-balances are enough to transform a corrupt practice culture into a healthy democracy. After decades of failed dictatorships and coups-d’état in post-colonial African democracies, we now see repeatedly the same story emerging time and again. Corruption and exploitation seem to “march on”. Civic associations whose aim is changing policies and improving governance are normally the first victims of such behavior. Therefore, efforts to improve government performance while transforming society are futile unless societies have access to laws against corruption, and the ability to enforce justice through the courts. phone. Smartphone thermal imagers are able to detect infrared (IR) light at different temperatures and scale them accordingly.
It’s known as a “thermal camera”. Many people call it an IR camera, but this is not quite accurate because you don’t require long wavelengths like the Infrared Light to see through smoke or fog; rather, these phones detect the IR spectrum which is invisible to humans (although some animals can also perceive it). For most applications, a smartphone can accurately record images up to about 400°F but higher temperatures vary from iPhone to iPhone – if you’re really keen on recording something above 68°F, then you’ll need an iOS device with a back camera set to “TrueColor” mode (more below).
The main problem with a smartphone’s ability to capture true color pictures is the amount of noise in their video signal due to poor processing power. To counteract this issue many smartphone manufacturers have added noise reduction technologies such as Digital Noise Reduction (DNR) and Hybrid Analog/Digital (HAD). These two types of filters work very differently though so let me show how they each handle reducing image quality.
The first step in determining whether your own model supports this feature would be checking manufacturer’s documentation online. Typical sources include Amazon.com / Best Buy Online Store , Apple Support Website , NerdWallet , Google Play App Market etc., although there might also be other resources depending on where you live (i.e.: international equivalents ).
What You Can Use It For
Most people use smartphones to take quick snapshots without any effort involved. Sometimes taking photos becomes complicated however when certain lighting conditions aren't optimal for our eyes. When shooting against direct sunlight we often get too much contrast between bright areas like windows vs dark ones behind us causing blurriness which distracts viewers instead of holding their attention towards what's happening inside said window itself! Also outdoor sports events rarely offer consistent levels of illumination throughout all four quarters making timing difficult even after all preparations have already taken place beforehand - hence why having access to wider angle cameras comes as handy especially since most times no single lens can provide sufficient coverage along one axis alone alone . This means sometimes you will come across situations where it simply isn't possible for someone else operating another machine just right next door!
In addition , using software applications programmed specifically for devices equipped with advanced capabilities such as automatic white balance adjustments alongside manual settings allows users much greater flexibility compared against traditional alternatives available today . Some apps enable front-facing features while others focus primarily around capturing low-light environments by utilizing algorithms designed specially for handling both cases separately whilst keeping things simple enough for anyone interested regardless of background knowledge regarding specific tech components involved .
How Does It Work?
Unlike digital cameras which convert photons directly into electrical signals within your eyeglasses frame , smartphone sensors rely heavily upon external optics combined together with custom built circuitry integrated onto silicon substrates forming an actual pixel matrix allowing receivers to read individual charge packets sent out during every single exposure cycle lasting about half second maximum depending on resolution

negotiated and long-delayed Middle East "road map" received a diplomatic boost by the recent intervention of George W. Bush, the plan is replete with the same structural flaws that doomed the Oslo Accords. Its primary weakness lies in its failure to provide sufficient resources to make it work. Although Washington claims the accord will be successful if Arab countries commit themselves to increased peace funding, much more must be done on both sides to set realistic paths toward a Palestinian state. The United States has been quick to blame the opposition of the Palestinians for delaying progress on the accord, although there are many obstacles facing them as well.

The second major flaw in the accord is the lack of a unified political authority or central government over all elements of security policy within Palestine and Israel. In theory, the accord provides each side access to the same institutions for negotiation and dispute resolution. Under actual conditions, however, Israeli forces control key border crossings into Gaza, where Hamas operates openly from dozens of strongholds and regularly engages in attacks against civilian populations. There is no doubt that Israel's security interests dictate some restrictions on freedom of movement between Palestine and Israel. But there should be greater transparency about these issues, and the accord should require Israel to grant other Palestinian groups certain guarantees in exchange for their cessation of violent activities and respect for the borders (including checkpoints). Likewise, Hamas should have better incentives to renounce violence and engage in constructive dialogue. Thus far, the accord hasn't lived up to critics' expectations; neither the Palestinian nor the Israeli leadership seems prepared to give up last-minute concessions needed to reach an agreement. Moreover, because the two sides can bargain only for present gains, the timetable runs the risk of breaking down before too many valuable compromises are reached.

The current crisis gives us an excellent opportunity--not to close our eyes to what goes wrong at the moment but to lay out the groundwork for change that may one day spell success. There is plenty of hope and motivation: Many people who once shunned the idea of a Palestinian state seem more open-minded now than they were just three months ago. More importantly, the recent change of regime in Cairo means Egypt will become more involved in helping build trust through economic cooperation rather than military campaigns. Saudi Arabia and the Gulf states also seem more committed to finding a way forward on their own.

Despite the efforts underway, the prospects are anything but clear. In the foreseeable future, we appear to be stuck fighting among ourselves. With every new setback, the question remains whether this road map really offers any real hope of bringing us back onto democratic tracks or building a viable Palestinian state, or simply another failed attempt at appeasing the masters of terror and inciting bloodshed in the region. Only time will tell which course history takes. For now, though, we shouldn't despair. We cannot afford to lose sight of those already risking so much. Even if the accord falls short of all ideals, the negotiations itself represent the first step in rebuilding a society built by Israelis and Palestinians working together

About the Book
Since its invention in 1888, X-rays have revolutionised medicine, changing public attitudes towards disease and trauma as well as surgery itself. For most of that century – until before the Second World War – they were largely used by physicists and engineers in their research, although there had been occasional attempts to exploit them for medical purposes, notably by Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen himself in 1895. After 1940, however, the number of applications steadily increased both within and beyond traditional medical circles. By then X-ray equipment had become more compact and portable, making it easier than ever to diagnose cancer from afar without risking patient privacy.
The first half of the book deals with medical applications developed during the First World War and the period following the war, when a new body known as Radiology came into existence. Because of wartime restrictions on flight, the advent of aviation brought radiological imaging techniques closer together. When these technologies began to be applied more freely to non-medical professions such as dentistry and art conservancy, or to industrial processes like metallurgy and textiles, major changes took place in what were by now many fields outside the purely scientific domain. Jean-François Couinaud created his anatomical segmentation system based on X-ray images, the principles of which are still essential to all modern surgical procedures today. In the second part of the story, the author looks at developments after the Second World War and considers some of the ways in which increasingly sophisticated imaging methods have affected the practices of disciplines ranging from criminology to forensic science and psychology to philosophy. Throughout, the historical narrative takes centre stage, and a wealth of illustrations accompany the text to give context and detail.
The Medical Revolution: A History of Radiology by Robert Halfon offers vivid insights into the history not only of medical practice but also of society as a whole. Through illuminating case histories readers can see clearly how discoveries about bodily structures revealed themselves to practitioners through ongoing debates among scientists, artists, inventors, doctors and restorers – sometimes causing major upheavals to conventional thinking and practice, and at other times being met with greater acceptance and respect than might otherwise appear possible. With the original contribution of a distinguished historian, THE MEDICAL REVOLUTION is not only a richly rewarding read but will also appeal equally to students and general readers looking for profound examples illustrating key intellectual trends in everyday life. The path of the historic hurricane is drawing comparisons to Maria and Irma, although there are clear differences. Not only was its size not anticipated, but here is where the similarities really begin:
A long swirl
Hurricane Florence was the longest-lasting tropical cyclone ever recorded anywhere on Earth by wind speed: It lingered for more than two weeks between landfall and cutting off its own circulation, ratcheting back into a depression that just didn't want to quit.
It had been building so strong for months that before making landfall near Wrightsville Beach, N.C., in late September 2018, Florence was an unusual beast among storms in that it wasn't driven by Atlantic Ocean water temperatures but rather by Gulf Stream currents. Its slow progression made northwestern Florida, Georgia and especially South Carolina vulnerable to inundation by what were then subsequently called four separate hurricanes.
Two weeks later another of those "four" groups of storms came through, this time with stronger winds and heavier rains.
The most extreme impact on record
Florence produced seven separate landfalls along the coast of North Carolina, all close enough together to suggest how devastating these twin storm systems would prove. In Charleston, S.C., rainfall totaled about 4 feet (including some localized amounts exceeding eight feet), and conditions there have persisted for several weeks. Hurricane-force gusts in Beaufort, North Carolina, blew at about 67 mph. There were dozens of tornadoes.
Florence was also distinctive because while most cyclones move out over open waters toward their decaying cores, this one remained relatively stationary, staying put over Central North America and bringing heavy rainfall to millions overland of Florida.
Tropical Storm Fay delivered 1 foot or more of rainfall during much of that period, and many residents of Florida saw up to six inches or more.
The toll of Hurricane Irene, though worse than anything we've seen so far, was surpassed by that sustained precipitation. Flooding and damage from the same high-intensity system happened in multiple counties across South Carolina, and the amount of rainfall was even longer lasting than Florence in parts of Texas and Louisiana.
Hurricane Harvey was known for torrential downpours, and it showed again with Tropical Depression Isabel after moving from Texas offshore eastward across Florida.
The wettest place on Earth
By comparison to Florence, Mexican typhoon Bopha made landfall over a decade earlier with slightly higher average daily rainfall of nearly five feet. In other words, all three storms were quite hefty, and certainly indicative of a tropical hazard of no small proportions.
Which brings us to Florence's successor: What will shape events for the foreseeable future?

You need to do this every week or two; at least once per month would be better. A 10-ounce spray bottle of water will easily hold about three months' value. Fill the bottle halfway to an inch below, then let the contents sit until clear over a period of several weeks. For the best effect, use distilled water instead.
For those unfortunate folks who have their showers without windows (I know some), open up the bathroom door as much as possible! To help them along, remind them to try turning left and right, swinging their hips, etc. After a short while, everyone learns to do this!
This is where the real magic happens. In most homes, the kitchen floor is higher than all other areas, because sinks, counters and cabinets usually take up more space near the kitchen faucet. This means that when we're trying to sweep out the germs and dirt on our surfaces, we often sweep in from underneath — i.e., dust and dirt get carried down by air currents. When cooking, even from a car window, we carry our cars' oils around with us because they hang in air currents. To counteract these natural pathways, buy a pair of rubber slippers (preferably slip-on types), which reduce friction so that any dust and oil you kick around won't fly into your eyes and mouth. Ideally, wear sneakers 90 percent of the time and flip flops 10 percent of the time (in summer, to sleep in) so you don't pick up too many bacteria. Your feet sweat, after all. Plus walking barefoot minimizes the amount of skin you put into contact with your floors, a practice recommended among health-conscious people since the late 60s — something similar may have saved Nancy Reagan, though she had other problems with her feet at times.

Now, tell me who has been drinking chlorinated tap water lately? Nobody. So why bother cleaning anything on your surface unless there's a strong scent -- such as cigarette smoke? If there are no smells, then you've probably already cleaned things thoroughly and can skip the rest. But what if you smell moldy socks and musty shoes? You could always make a quick trip to Wal-Mart's hardware section, purchase some fresh breath bleach, and create an effective cleaner.

In his defence strategy for Euro 2016 last month in France, the man nicknamed "Mannschafts-Master" seemed more patient than angry: he wanted to build trust through long periods of preparation; to give his stars time to recover from injuries; to play matches without losing ground, and to let the game unfold slowly rather than by resorting to frenzied counter-attacking.
This approach created some early doubts, though, because Germans often do not like to give themselves time – and the less able to take risks and make mistakes – before hitting hard. The first component of reaching a large audience without overwhelming everyone is knowing exactly what you want to accomplish. SnapChat CEO Evan Spiegel talked about their approach to building this: “We realized we couldn’t do something that was cool now if we knew we wouldn't see enough users come back later”, he explained at TechCrunch‘s SXSW Interactive conference last month. In other words, when the app was first released early this year, the focus was on getting as many people using SnapChat as possible by making it easy to use even as an anonymous account.
“Evolution” had been a big part of Snapchat’s success from day one, and the app has seen regular upgrades from 1.0 through to version 6. There is no doubt Snapchat has done its homework regarding designing products that resonate with consumers. For example, the ability to save snaps into a “story” format allows users to play with photography longer than ever before which only makes them more likely to return.
Snapchat goes further though because they not only keep an eye on user behavior – identifying which features work best based on real data – but also incorporate feedback directly into future updates. When Snapchat first started releasing new versions of the app, the designers would solicit suggestions for things to improve or add in the existing software from current users. The team then conducted small A/B tests (sometimes known as split testing) around certain design aspects or content changes over a two-week period, and incorporated the results directly into subsequent releases. Understandably so, most companies avoid doing this sort of thing since it takes extra effort and requires resources beyond what is needed to create an update. Therefore it is quite surprising to learn that someone at Snapchat actually does it every single release!
This continuous cycle between feature updates and soliciting suggestions gives Snapchat loyalists access to something very few apps offer: constant improvement in product functionality. Productivity improves, and the amount of attention a brand receives increases as a direct result.
If that wasn’t clear enough, Snapchat has also made sure those updates benefit all users regardless of whether they pay for optional in-app services. For example, there are some cases where additional paid subscriptions allow enhanced privacy settings for camera photos. With so much built-in innovation, it is really difficult to imagine changing anything at all.
For companies wanting to maximize the impact of their messages online but still encourage engagement, these digital marketing strategies should be taken to heart. No matter the budget, leveraging cutting-edge technology while listening to customer demand offers great potential. Don’t expect innovation and strategy to happen overnight though; rather, plan ahead and act decisively when opportunities arise.

In 2005, the same procedure was also successfully performed in Australia's Royal Melbourne Children's Hospital; but experts there had not offered a detailed description of its particulars until now.
Although similar procedures were previously developed and practiced around the world, the new technique features some important innovations that enhance surgical safety and success. For example, the modified approach reduces the potential risk that surgeons might encounter if tissue accidentally encases or surrounds one of the ureters, which are responsible for draining urine out of the body. Although complications such as this can be common with repair surgeries involving the bladder, they could potentially be serious if the ureter is compromised.
According to Dicker -- who joined the staff of the University of Chicago Medicine in July of last year as senior lecturer -- the modified version of the surgery involves several steps that reduce the likelihood of complications:
- Patients are initially placed under general anesthesia before the bladder is partially detached without removing any part of the anatomy.
- Next, the surgeon inserts a robotic probe through the rectum into a cavity between the bladder (called a pelviureterostomy) and places catheters inside the bladder and the ureters to divert urine away while restoring blood flow to the ureters following the surgery.
- Finally, the bladder is completely separated from adjacent tissues as a wide "sling" is formed over both sides of the bladder via small incisions above the pubic bone and the ureters are carefully guided toward their usual course down past the bladder.
Based on results achieved so far, Dicker believes patients undergoing the advanced robot-assisted surgery typically recover faster, have less pain compared to live-tissue techniques commonly employed today.
He says, "In addition to providing greater access and visibility during surgery, the technique eliminates the need for full removal of the bladder, reducing the amount of bleeding and postoperative pain that may otherwise result." He notes another advantage of the modified approach is that surgeons have more time to perform close observation of the ureters because they no longer must cut away surrounding tissue after beginning the operation. Dicker and his team conduct robotics training programs to educate pediatric urologists across North America, Europe, the Middle East and Asia.

The shifting climate among residents of big cities could mean that, unlike Calgary and Edmonton, the BC real estate industry doesn’t seem likely to recover any time soon.
The current slump came after the price gains recorded through the end of 2015 triggered a government ban on local speculators buying properties worth $2 million or more. The provincial government implemented this policy because it wanted to quell demand before the value of those homes rose too far above their underlying values.
It is not yet clear whether such policies can really work. Real change begins when the supply exceeds demand. When the market becomes less competitive, it will be more difficult for developers to build, and builders need customers.
For now however, the problem seems to stem mainly from buyers. Many people who were interested in getting a house are no longer willing to pay what they know is an inflated amount.
Concerns about affordability also seem to play a factor here. In many places across North America, average mortgage payments now exceed wages; rent-to-income ratios are high; shortfalls between available and needed affordable units often amount to thousands. As a result, we’re seeing less consumer spending, fewer businesses opening up, and fewer positive business outcomes. It puts downward pressure on income growth for individuals.
Selling your home means you buy another product: You’ve traded one asset for another, usually of inferior quality. After you put down a first deposit on a new property, you’ll probably find yourself stuck at checkout in the same department store where you had your last deal break.
You wait until the price drops for sale again only to discover that – since the price you paid will always be higher – you received good value for your money originally. Then you learn that, despite selling on top of a substantial discount, the old property was still fully booked when you bought it.
You may not understand why prices stayed artificially inflated even after the starters gave the market the message “buyers beware.” Perhaps speculative projects tempted people with a visible promise of easy profits. Maybe banks encouraged borrowers who did not understand the risks associated with financing large amounts of money easily.
Perhaps developers knew there would be plenty of potential buyers waiting for their first opportunity to invest. Or possibly even the reverse: Buyers did just fine in spite of very expensive mortgages offered by banks. So perhaps the idea of investing money instead of trading it was seen as better overall than not making much money in the process. An appeals court Wednesday rejected an attempt by nearly half the nation's patent offices and the Patent and Trademark Office to stop allowing companies displaying on computer screens "mathematical formulas that produce a saleable result," according to an announcement.
The ruling is the final decision in what was one of the most compelling patent cases in recent history — until now. In 1978, a company named Digital Equipment Corp., in Maynard, Mass., won a federal appeals court's ruling saying that as long as a device or process actually produces money for its owner or users, the computer program may not be considered merely an idea but a patent-eligible invention capable of providing exclusive commercial advantage over those who have not yet invented the same process. If approved by other branch agencies and the Patent and Trademark Office, such products could provide significant new opportunities for innovation and industry, advocates say.
The company's claim of exclusivity depends upon the method used in the program, known as LOGO (Language Oriented Graphics). The first version of the system was designed in 1967 at MIT with help from researchers at Apple Computer Inc. in Cupertino, Calif. In 1970, the two firms merged and began promoting software programs based on the language's capability to allow a child the ability to draw or graphically manipulate equations in a computer. If one examines U.S. history from 1900 to present day, there are clear trends evident:
- From about 1900 through the First World War—a period marked by two global conflicts—America’s population and economy expanded rapidly. The armed forces grew in size, and postwar military spending generated new economic growth for America. During the same period, the nation had established its leading position in high tech markets like automobiles, aircraft manufacturing, electrical power generation, and shipbuilding. Innovation and technological advancements were becoming characteristic features of modern business practice; indeed, the United States emerged as an example of “the good life” for all who experienced it.
- From World War I through the Korean conflict—the period marking America’s entry into a long succession of Cold War battles between communism and freedom—the population continued expanding and the nation took up arms against totalitarian regimes or fascist states. There was also great interest in national defense programs that ushered in what would become the Golden Age of Technology. According to “The Age of Conquest,” a book published by C. Robert Colihan and Edward Humes in 2000, “During the Second World War, American industrial production rose by nearly five times.” Certainly many people could not afford these advanced products, but a big number did, and Americans enthusiastically purchased them.
- From 1967 through the late 1980s—an era of heightened tensions with two superpowers locked in nuclear war, the Soviet Union invaded Czechoslovakia and attempted to partition Afghanistan, and the Viet Cong waged guerrilla warfare in South Vietnam—there was much frustration among some elements of society regarding atrocities perpetrated against innocent civilians. There was widespread concern that terrorist actions aimed at western countries might lead to an all-out war with Russia. Not surprisingly, the nation, without any real warning, entered into a “hot civil war” that resulted in approximately four million deaths, the total equivalent of a large city’s population being wiped out in less than three decades.
The Cold War
World War III never broke out during this thirty-year time period (from 1945 to the late 1967), yet the world seemed to spend every conceivable hour abuzz with talk of imminent destruction. After the Soviet Union invaded Poland in 1939 and started World War II, the communist nations’ geographic borders became unstable. Following Japan’s attack on Pearl Harbor in Hawaii in December 1941, the United States entered the war and immediately faced another challenge: whether to declare war if the USSR declared war first. Its leader Fidel Castro wanted Cuba’s independence from the United States, and the Russians showed no interest in supporting Cuban independence from the United States, or maintaining close diplomatic relations. # 1


The answer was simple enough: “Because when you know something true…,” one student began, “you can share your experience with someone else.” Another student took over, “and then they’ll get this idea too!” A few more students agreed that learning could contribute to social change—perhaps by changing policies or laws—because once you had an understanding of what needed to change, you could push forward change until those things were changed.

The first two answers point to personal benefits of learning. There is a strong link between knowledge—or information—received through reading and rote memorization (reading comprehension) and strong academic achievement (including grades). But what about universal experiences shared across societies and cultures?


# 2

Another student raised his hand and added, “Because what you know helps you solve problems better.”

A lot of us have experienced being in trouble at some point in our lives. In these situations, there are countless reasons not to do anything. For instance:

  • If I’m angry at another person, maybe speaking up won’t help much.
  • If I’m scared, doing as anyone tells me will cause my fear to grow even worse.
  • If my family members don’t support me, going along might hurt their feelings more than mine.

And yet sometimes we choose the right course of action none the less.

The students who raised this issue made the same argument about helping others around us: “If we truly understand a situation or problem, we can act smartly and appropriately for all concerned.”

#3 And finally:

“What you know affects how you behave toward other people.”

An important aspect of teaching ethics—and informed morality—is recognizing different viewpoints. For example, we might try to convince someone who doesn’t believe in eating meat to give up meat completely to save animals’ lives. A Skin Tag Is Really a Flesh Ball
Regardless of its name, a tag is just normal little flesh ball growing away from your skin. Normally, these growths grow out on top of your skin and are either raised like a bumpy pea, or smooth but still raised like a dewdrop. However, there are also types of tags that grow below skin level. There are even those that grow under both eyelids at once because they're super sensitive! In most cases, skin tags will show no signs whatsoever unless there are more than 50 present in an individual. So how do you know whether the little skin balls near your eyes aren't anything else?
Well, the answer lies in their location.
The Most Common Types Of Tags Are:
- Junctional Cysts And Subcutaneous Cysts: These are the two types of tags that appear beneath the skin and have soft tissue lying above them. You may also refer to them as duct tumors, epidermal hyperplasia cysts or basal cell papillomas. More commonly known by patients is the term funnel-shaped tumor which refers to tags that grow along the hair line behind the earlobe or atop of the head.
- Benign Malignant Melanotic Macules: Though not technically tags themselves, benign malignant melanotic macules are examples of a type of lesion that appears on the chest, stomach, neck and arms where the pigment cells produce excess amounts of melanin due to sun exposure. They can be either flat or dome shaped with irregular borders and can sometimes feel hard to the touch.

Now, under new leadership from Lisa McCurry, the Irvine Foundation Program is adapting to changing demands after COVID-19 and fine-tuning its offerings to give more students access to postsecondary education — work that could help all ages fill jobs heavily impacted by this year’s economic downturn.
“COVID really reinforced our need to add additional types of educational opportunities,” McCurry said.
New programs include enrollment assistance, financial aid, mentoring, academic coaching and peer-to-peer connections among fellow students who have already graduated. "The SCE is not a red-herring," said Mike Chase, director of vulnerability research at Microsoft. "What it does very early after a new version gets out the door, and what we have seen with our customers...is if there are some security holes and vulnerabilities that may not be fully patched or discovered, then this report from us helps you find those before they end up in users hands."
"It basically allows them to discover these flaws much quicker than if we had just rolled them out without building this type of tool into our products, and made it available for free to everybody on earth to use," he added. "That way we can get rid of unnecessary threat surface."
Microsoft also plans to allow developers to distribute tools such as SCE - which will provide support for checking product quality, identifying known problems and improving software throughout its life cycle - through the Software Development Kit portion of its Web site.
Chase said the idea behind SCE is that instead of running protocols against everything the company develops, the system first checks whether the application is properly configured to receive new updates. If so, then it applies patches and starts testing again.
If, on the other hand, the application is not configured properly, or the engineer using that platform did not follow the same naming convention as was used when the app was coded, then any changes made during development would not apply correctly, resulting in flawed targets being sent to production systems where users could unknowingly come across poorly fixed issues. In the latter case, the system allows developers to fix their errors manually rather than throwing the entire system away to reinstall older versions of code.
Chase said SCE is analogous to how people tend to handle kitchen appliances like microwaves: You connect them, plug them in, and your job is done - unless something goes wrong. Then you turn down the dial, reboot the microwave, and try it again.
He said his group will be working closely with Redmond partner Jesse Turner next week to test the new SCE tool in various environments. It does this solely to learn from any mistakes it might make while going into customers' offices.

But what do you call the true account of how Western intelligence services did, systematically and brutally, without remorse, everything they could think up to contain information deemed too dangerous to disseminate? This story has yet to receive adequate treatment in books which are rather thin on Cold War drama.


This look at the authors’ strategies reveals why certain ways of producing literature seem more effective than others, and why certain pieces become classic works while others languish in obscurity. Novels may be read and discussed but will readers remember them till death?


I am a sociologist who often writes novels to explore complex ideas from a historical perspective. I see writing as a way of “seeing” history—through the metaphorical lenses I weave between my other forms of analysis. I’m particularly interested in exploring how larger social forces impact people: whether the media affects public attitudes toward issues such as cancer research, or the role of art and literature in shaping popular culture. I’ve seen that changing societal norms can shape our moral sensibilities. For instance, the idea of a woman’s place being in a house once defined women’s experiences. And what’s fascinating to me is that those norms change over time.

If we’re willing to spend money on art and literature, we shouldn’t just assume it’s for entertainment purposes alone. When choosing books, filmmakers and publishers must also consider important cultural and historical factors. After Donald Trump won the US election in November, a number of established literary greats graced white houses during an otherwise dismal week for American booksellers. So the question remains: does this assumption reflect reality?

How much better off we humans may be if we chose our movies based less on star power or box-office success—and instead aimed for our productions to pay tribute to different cultures and human emotions through a greater understanding of art’s potential. Fictionalised history has stood strong in cinema as a result: think Ben Hur, Mr Bean, or the recent Star Wars films.

As political science scholars debate whether women will be better candidates than men, or will cause their parties to lose out on power by standing in what is now a male-dominated presidential field, a new study shows that the answer may rest on which party's candidates' female members each side see as more desirable.
The findings point to an interesting dynamic in Western democracies where the number of seats won by both sexes at national elections appears balanced when it comes to winning office — but significantly off-kilter among parliamentary candidates from individual parties. In short, those countries with low female representation at the ballot box often have high female electoral momentum at the national level. This trend is mirrored within party ranks: Male MPs tend to favour fellow males; Female MPs, meanwhile, seem to unite around one woman.
"Unsurprisingly, we find that women politics is much stronger inside the legislature," says lead author Jennifer Audunson, a sociologist at Indiana University Bloomington. "What's less obvious is how this might reflect outside the legislature."
Labour versus Loyalists
Wealthy families have long been allies with parliamentary representatives in the UK, a relationship known as patronage. But politics also traditionally works through a private web of relationships between parliamentarians and their constituents, exposing legislators to ideas about politics coming not only from their colleagues, but directly from constituency voters.
It was none other than former Labour leader Tony Blair whose 2005 election campaign successfully tapped into support for women politicians. For a decade, the British government had seen very little change in parliamentary representation at all — until the emergence of modern-day "lamborians", a generation of people who were born after the Second World War and disproportionately female.
The influx of these "lady lambors", which became increasingly popular thanks to the success of Blair's 1997 leadership bid, created strong pressure on lawmakers to focus on getting females elected to Parliament over achieving ministerial positions inside the Palace of Westminster. After taking office in July 2003, the Conservatives clumsily exploited this dynamic in order to win nearly half the seats across constituencies they contested in May 2005.
This led to an interesting phenomenon. With the right strategy, a female MP could win slightly above the statistical chance of gaining a seat without any extra campaigning. Research suggests that female MPs did indeed do just that during the latter period of the Labour administration. Their presence in local legislatures helped create an environment where more female MPs were elected elsewhere in Britain, though evidence suggests they failed to carry over their numbers in female-dominated areas.
A similar story emerged when the Liberals took control of Hong Kong's Legislative Council under then-provisional leader Carrie Lam. The cost of drug treatments is usually paid through what's called out-of-pocket expenses or "copays," which are calculated as a percentage of a prescribed treatment per prescription. Or they could come from premiums and deductibles charged for medical services themselves. For many patients with high-deductible health insurance plans, the copay or deductible can eat up all or most of their savings.
And while most insurers have expanded prescription coverage so people don't end up paying thousands every month for medication, there's still too much overlap between their networks and the pharmacy benefit managers who negotiate prices -- especially on brand-name drugs that are higher-priced at generic equivalents on the market already.
The result: tens of thousands of Americans who still have to pay thousands a year even when they're insured. In 2013 alone the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau found 47 states had uncovered $69 million spent by people on out-of-pocket pharmacy costs because they were using unaffordable medications due to lack of acceptable alternative options on the market.
If you've ever felt stuck buying one-store-brand drugs no matter how little your plan pays, consider some steps you might take:
If you need to cover an extensive list of prescription medications each month, ask your doctor if she can get you generic versions of a few costly prescriptions (in other words, nonbrand medicines) instead. Generic drugs are available in every region of the country and typically contain slightly different ingredients than branded drugs. But doctors aren't required to prescribe generics since they must prescribe the FDA-approved medicine with exacting specifications such as dosage, strength, concentration, etc., if the same active ingredient used in a brand-name product exists. So choose alternatives only after consulting with your physician.
Prove your claim
Many insurance companies charge higher co-pays based on the number of prescription medications you need per day. Check with your insurer and make sure those claims are being billed accordingly; this practice may also be known as an "excess" policy — meaning that someone else will pay part of your bill if certain requirements are met.
If your plan doesn't allow generic medications in its network, contact pharmacies that operate outside its coverage area. Some are directly affiliated with major national drug chains like CVS Caremark and Walgreens, and others accept payment for out-of-network prescriptions from private insurance companies. This way you'll be able to save money on prescriptions without having to change your plan.
Using "buyers markets"
One strategy is to buy names brand products under different trade names that manufacturers license to other firms.
